0.title: In Christ
0.essay:
Two small words run through the New Testament like a golden thread: “in Christ”. Paul uses them, with “in him” and “in the Lord”, again and again. They are easy to read past, yet they describe the heart of being a Christian.

More than following Jesus

Many think of a Christian as someone who admires Jesus and tries to live as he lived. The New Testament says something far deeper: a Christian has been joined to Christ, so that what is his becomes theirs. “And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

Reformed teaching calls this union with Christ. John Calvin made the point at the start of his teaching on how salvation reaches us: as long as Christ stays outside us and we are separated from him, all that he suffered and did for our salvation is of no use to us. A Saviour admired from a distance cannot save us; we need one we are joined to.

The hub of the wheel

Union with Christ is not one blessing among many. It is the hub from which every other blessing runs like a spoke: being chosen, forgiven, declared righteous, adopted, made holy, kept, comforted in suffering, and raised at the last day. Each is ours because we are in him. Other studies treat several of these spokes; this one shows how they hold together in one living Lord.

The chapters

Chosen in Him: what it means to be in Christ; Vine, Body and Bride: the pictures Scripture uses, and what the union is not; Every Blessing in Him: justification, adoption and holiness; Held in Him: perseverance and suffering; One Body, One Bread: union, the church and the Lord’s Supper; and The Dead in Christ: death, resurrection and glory. For further reading: Calvin’s Institutes 3.1 and 3.11; the Westminster Larger Catechism, questions 65 to 69; John Murray, Redemption Accomplished and Applied; and J. Todd Billings, Union with Christ.

For reflection

If someone asked you what makes a person a Christian, what would you say? Would your answer include being joined to Christ himself?

1.title: Chosen in Him: What It Means to Be in Christ
1.essay:
“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:3–4).

One phrase, over and over

Read Ephesians 1:3–14 slowly and count the phrases: “in Christ”, “in him”, “in the Beloved”. Paul cannot stop saying it. God chose us “in him” (Ephesians 1:4). “In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (Ephesians 1:7). “In him we have obtained an inheritance” (Ephesians 1:11). And “in him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13). Every blessing Paul names is found in one place: in Christ.

God does not hand out blessings as separate parcels. He gives us his Son, and in his Son he gives us everything.

Two heads

To see why this matters, Paul takes us back to the beginning. The whole human race was bound up with one man, Adam. When he fell, we fell with him. “For as by the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). And again: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

Every person stands “in” someone. By nature we are in Adam: his guilt is counted to us and his corruption passed on. By grace believers are moved into Christ, the head of a new humanity. What he did, he did as our representative, and what he won, he won for those in him. This is often called our federal or covenant union with Christ.

Planned, won and applied

Scripture speaks of this union in three stages. It was planned in eternity: God chose us “in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4), so that before we existed, the Father looked on his people as belonging to his Son. It was won in history: when Christ died and rose, he did so as the head of his people, so that Paul can say believers died and were raised with him. And it is applied in our own lives when the Spirit brings us to faith: “when you heard … and believed in him, were sealed” (Ephesians 1:13).

Because the union was planned in eternity, it does not depend on us. Because it was won at the cross, it rests on a finished work. Because it is applied in time, there was a day when we who were “dead in our trespasses” were “made … alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:5).

The bond: the Spirit and faith

How is a person on earth joined to a Saviour who is in heaven? Scripture gives two answers that belong together. From God’s side, the bond is the Holy Spirit. “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9), and “by this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit” (1 John 4:13). The Spirit who filled Christ comes to live in his people, and so joins the members to the head.

From our side, the bond is faith. Paul prays “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:17). Faith is not a work that earns union. It is the empty hand the Spirit opens, the act of a sinner receiving Christ. The hand that grips a rope thrown to a drowning man does not save him, but it receives the one who does.

The Larger Catechism (question 66) puts it simply: the union is the work of God’s grace, by which the elect are spiritually, really and inseparably joined to Christ as their head and husband, and it is done in their effectual calling.

Why it matters

Here Calvin’s point comes into its own. Christ’s life, death and resurrection are the ground of our salvation, but a treasure locked in a bank we have no claim on does not make us rich. The good news is not only that Christ did all this, but that through the Spirit and faith he becomes ours, and we become his.

A man in his forties had been in church all his life. He thought of Christianity as a set of good teachings that he was trying, with mixed success, to follow. When a home group studied Ephesians 1, he was struck by how little of it was about his effort. Everything was “in him”. He said it felt as if he had read the instructions on the box for years and only now opened it to find a person inside.

The Father chose us in his Son before the world began. The Son took our nature, stood in our place and rose as our head. The Spirit joined us to him. The whole Trinity is at work to make us one with Christ. That is a love we will spend eternity exploring.

For reflection

Read Ephesians 1:3–14 and list every blessing Paul says is ours “in him”. What difference does it make that you were once “in Adam” and are now “in Christ”? Why is it important that faith receives Christ rather than earns him? How might you thank God this week for each person of the Trinity’s part in joining you to Christ?

2.title: Vine, Body and Bride: Pictures of the Union
2.essay:
How do you describe something no human relationship fully matches? Scripture does not give one picture of our union with Christ but several, each showing a different side of the same reality. And it also shows us where the pictures stop.

The vine and the branches

On the night before he died, Jesus said, “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). A branch does not produce its own life. The sap that flows through the vine flows through it. Cut off, it withers. Joined, it bears fruit.

This is a picture of life. The union is not only a legal arrangement; it is living. Christ’s life flows into his people by his Spirit. And the picture carries a call: “Abide in me, and I in you” (John 15:4). We abide by trusting his word, obeying his commands and resting in his love (John 15:7–10). Jesus’ aim is warm: “that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full” (John 15:11).

The head and the body

Paul’s favourite picture is the body. Christ “is the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18). From the head “the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love” (Ephesians 4:16).

This is a picture of rule and belonging. The head directs the body; the body depends on the head. It also means that Christ feels what happens to his people. When Saul was hunting Christians, the risen Lord asked him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Not “my followers”, but “me”.

The bridegroom and the bride

The most intimate picture is marriage. In the Old Testament the Lord spoke to his people as a husband: “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hosea 2:19). In the New Testament Paul quotes the words of Genesis about two becoming one flesh, and then says, “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). History ends with a wedding: “the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).

This is a picture of love and shared possession. Our sin and debts became his to bear; his righteousness and riches become ours to enjoy. Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), and he does not divorce his bride.

Living stones

Peter adds a building. Coming to Christ, the living cornerstone, “you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5). Paul says the same: “In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). This is a picture of God’s presence: joined to Christ, his people become the place where God lives.

Real, but not a merging

Because the union is so close, some have described it in ways that go too far. Here are the main views.

Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of theosis or deification, drawing on 2 Peter 1:4, where believers “become partakers of the divine nature”. Orthodox teachers are careful to say that we share in God’s energies, his life and activity, and never in his essence; a human being never becomes God by nature. Some forms of popular mysticism, both inside and outside the church, go much further and speak of the soul being absorbed into God like a drop into the ocean, or of discovering that we were divine all along. At the other end, some Christians reduce union to a legal arrangement or to agreement with Jesus’ teaching, with no real sharing of life at all.

This commentary’s view: union with Christ is real, personal and spiritual, worked by the Holy Spirit and received by faith. It is both legal (Christ is our representative, and what is his is counted ours) and vital (his life flows into us). It is closer than any human bond, and it can never be broken. But it is not a merging of beings. Christ remains the eternal Son, and we remain creatures, forever dependent and forever distinct. When the Larger Catechism calls it mystical, it means real and beyond our full understanding, not that we lose ourselves in God. In 2 Peter 1:4 Peter is speaking of escaping corruption and sharing God’s moral likeness and life through his promises, not of becoming divine. The bride does not become the bridegroom; the branch does not become the vine.

A university student who had dabbled in meditation told her pastor that she wanted to “lose herself in God”. He gently pointed her to Ephesians 5. The goal of the gospel is not that you vanish, he said, but that you are loved, named and kept by Christ forever, more fully yourself than you have ever been. That is better than absorption: it is communion.

For reflection

Which of the pictures (vine, body, bride, building) speaks most to you at present, and why? What does Acts 9:4 tell you about how closely Christ identifies with his people? Why does it matter that we are never absorbed into God? What does it mean for you to “abide” in Christ this week?

3.title: Every Blessing in Him: Justification, Adoption and Holiness
3.essay:
Christ “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). Notice that Paul does not say Christ gives us these things as if they were separate from him. He became them for us. Have Christ, and you have them all.

Christ is not divided

Salvation has many parts: justification, adoption, sanctification, glorification. It is helpful to distinguish them, and Reformed teaching is careful to do so. But they never come apart, because they are all found in one person. Calvin spoke of a double grace that we receive by being joined to Christ: being reconciled to God through his blamelessness, and being made holy by his Spirit. You cannot have one half of Christ. The Christ who forgives is the Christ who transforms.

This guards against two errors: thinking that forgiveness makes holiness unimportant, and thinking that we must become holy before God will accept us. In him we are accepted completely, and in him we are being changed truly.

Righteous in him

“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Here is the great exchange. Our sin was reckoned to Christ; his righteousness is reckoned to us. Paul longed to “gain Christ and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ” (Philippians 3:8–9).

Union does not make justification depend on what Christ does inside us. The verdict rests entirely on what Christ did for us, outside us, on the cross. But union explains why that righteousness can be justly counted ours: we are joined to the one who earned it, as a bride shares her husband’s name and estate. So “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). The study The Doctrines of Grace treats justification more fully.

Sons in the Son

“For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith” (Galatians 3:26). Jesus is the eternal Son of the Father by nature. We become sons and daughters by adoption, and we do so only because we are in him. “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15).

The Father’s love for his people is not a second-class love. Jesus prayed that the world may know that the Father “sent me and loved them even as you loved me” (John 17:23). We are loved in the Beloved. And we are “heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17): what the Son inherits, his brothers and sisters share.

Dead to sin, alive to God

Union is also the root of holiness. “We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). When Christ died, his people died with him to sin’s reign. When he rose, they rose with him to a new life. So Paul says, “consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:11). The study Fighting Sin & Temptation works this out in detail.

Paul’s own testimony is the clearest summary: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). Notice that Paul still lives, and still believes. Christ does not replace him; Christ lives in him and through him.

This changes how we fight sin. Holiness is not an attempt to become someone we are not. It is learning to live as who we already are in Christ. “If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is” (Colossians 3:1). The command rests on the fact. We are “created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians 2:10), and the vine produces the fruit.

Trying harder, or abiding?

A young mother had come to faith a few years before. She felt she was failing as a Christian: impatient with her children, inconsistent in prayer, quick to compare herself with others. Her approach was simply to try harder, and she was exhausted. An older woman in her church read Romans 6 and John 15 with her over several weeks. The question changed from “How can I make myself better?” to “Who am I in Christ, and how do I draw on him?” She still struggled, but she began to pray honestly, confess quickly and expect growth as the fruit of a living union rather than the reward of willpower. Her effort did not stop; it was given a new root.

How rich the Saviour is! He did not merely open a door and leave us to walk through. He gave himself, and with himself pardon, sonship, a new heart and a sure inheritance.

For reflection

Why does it matter that justification and sanctification are distinct but never separate? What does it mean to you that the Father loves you “even as” he loves his Son? How does Galatians 2:20 shape the way you think about your own efforts to grow? Which sin might you face this week by remembering who you are in Christ?

4.title: Held in Him: Perseverance and Suffering
4.essay:
“Because I live, you also will live” (John 14:19). Jesus spoke those words to frightened disciples on the night he was betrayed. Our life is tied to his. As long as he lives, those who are in him are safe.

As secure as the one who holds us

The security of the believer is not a separate doctrine bolted on to the gospel. It flows from union. If we are joined to Christ, then to lose us he would have to lose a part of his own body. That is why Paul’s great list ends where it does: nothing “in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). The love is in Christ Jesus. It is as unbreakable as he is.

Jesus says of his sheep, “I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). The study Assurance of Salvation explores these promises fully. Here the point is simple: our hold on Christ is weak, but his hold on us is not. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

This does not make holiness optional. Jesus warned that a branch that bears no fruit is “thrown away like a branch and withers” (John 15:6). Those who finally fall away were never truly joined to the vine; they were near it, not in it. Real union always shows itself in real, if imperfect, fruit.

Comfort for ordinary believers

Union with Christ is not a privilege for spiritual high-achievers. The newest believer and the oldest saint are equally in Christ. The one who prays with fire and the one who can barely pray at all are joined to the same head. Your feelings may rise and fall, but the union does not.

Christ “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). Think of the most ordinary, struggling, forgettable Christian you know, perhaps yourself. The Son of God is not ashamed of that person. He has bound himself to them for ever.

Sharing his sufferings

Union with Christ also means sharing his path. We are “fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him” (Romans 8:17). Paul wanted to “know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share his sufferings, becoming like him in his death” (Philippians 3:10). Peter tells suffering believers to “rejoice insofar as you share Christ’s sufferings, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed” (1 Peter 4:13).

This does not mean our suffering adds anything to Christ’s atoning work, which was finished on the cross. When Paul speaks of “filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body” (Colossians 1:24), he means the sufferings the church still endures as the gospel spreads, sufferings which Christ counts as his own because his people are his body. It means that the Christian’s pain is never meaningless and never lonely. The head feels what the body feels. And because we suffer with him, we will be glorified with him. The road that goes through Gethsemane and Golgotha ends at the empty tomb.

And there is comfort on the road itself: “For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too” (2 Corinthians 1:5).

When the darkness is deep

Some suffering is in the mind. A believer can be truly joined to Christ and still face depression, anxiety or despair. Union with Christ does not mean such struggles are signs of failure, nor that medicine or a doctor’s care is a lack of faith. If you are struggling, speak to your doctor and to a trusted person in your church. If you are thinking of ending your life, please seek help now: call the emergency services or a crisis line, or tell someone you trust today. Christ holds you in the dark as surely as in the light.

A man in a hospital bed

A man in his sixties was told that his illness could not be cured. In the weeks that followed he found it hard to pray, and he worried that his faith was failing. A friend read to him from Romans 8 and John 14. What struck him was not that he must hold on more tightly, but that he was held. “I live because he lives,” he said. “That is not going to change when my body stops.” His fear did not vanish overnight, but it was answered.

That is the wonder of it. The Son of God, who upholds the universe, has bound himself to weak and suffering people, and he will not let them go.

For reflection

How does union with Christ make the believer’s security as firm as Christ’s own life? Why is it a comfort that the weakest believer is as truly in Christ as the strongest? How might seeing your suffering as a sharing in Christ’s sufferings change the way you bear it? Who in your church needs to hear that Christ is not ashamed of them?

5.title: One Body, One Bread: Union, the Church and the Lord’s Supper
5.essay:
No one is joined to Christ alone. To be united to the head is to be united to the body. The same union that joins us to Christ joins us to every other believer.

Joined to him, joined to each other

“For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12). Notice the last words: not “so it is with the church”, but “so it is with Christ”. Christ and his people are so closely bound that Paul can call them together by his name.

The Spirit who joins us to Christ is the same Spirit who forms the body: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body … and all were made to drink of one Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:13). That is why the walls that divide people elsewhere fall in the church. “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). This does not erase the differences God made, such as man and woman; it means none of them gives anyone a higher standing in Christ.

This is the root of the communion of saints: sharing in Christ, believers share with one another their gifts, burdens and joys. The 1689 Baptist Confession begins its chapter on the communion of saints with union with Christ, and draws from it the duty of believers to serve one another’s good, inwardly and outwardly. A Christian who says, “I love Christ but I do not need the church” is like a hand that says it loves the head but has no use for the arm.

Baptism: the sign of union

Christ gave two ordinances, and both speak of union. Baptism is the sign of entry. “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). Paul uses it to picture our burial and rising with Christ (Romans 6:3–4).

This commentary holds that baptism does not create the union; faith in Christ, worked by the Spirit, does. Baptism is the God-given sign and seal of a union that already exists by faith, so closely tied to the reality that Scripture can speak of the sign as if it did the thing it signifies. That is one reason this commentary baptises believers: the sign belongs to those who have come to Christ. Brothers and sisters who baptise infants are honoured fellow members of the one body.

The Lord’s Supper: feeding on Christ

If baptism marks the beginning of union, the Lord’s Supper nourishes it. “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:16–17). The word translated “participation” is the word for fellowship or sharing. At the table believers share in Christ, and in sharing in him, they share in one another.

Christians understand Christ’s presence at the Supper differently. Roman Catholics teach transubstantiation: the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood in substance. Lutherans hold that Christ’s body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many evangelicals see the Supper chiefly as a memorial, a vivid act of remembering. The Reformed view, which this commentary holds, is that Christ is truly present by his Spirit, and believers truly feed on him by faith, while the bread and wine remain bread and wine. It is a memorial, and more: communion with a living Lord. The study The Church weighs these views.

Union explains why this matters. In John 6 Jesus says, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). In context he is speaking of believing in him, for “whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). The Supper does not add a second way of being joined to Christ. It is a visible word, given by Christ to strengthen the union that faith already enjoys. As the body is fed by bread, so the soul is fed by Christ.

At the table

A widow in her seventies had stopped coming to church after her husband died, feeling invisible and alone. A deacon visited and invited her back. Her first Sunday back was a communion Sunday. As she took the bread with people she barely knew, she remembered the words “we who are many are one body”. She said later that she had been grieving as if she had no family, and at the table she discovered that she had a large one.

What a Saviour, who not only joins us to himself but gives us one another, and who meets us at his table with bread and wine to say again, “This is my body, which is for you” (1 Corinthians 11:24).

For reflection

Why does union with Christ make membership of a local church more than optional? What does 1 Corinthians 10:16–17 teach about what happens when believers share the Supper? How might you prepare your heart differently for the Lord’s Supper next time? Who in your church might feel invisible, and how could you show them they belong to the body?

6.title: The Dead in Christ: Death, Resurrection and Glory
6.essay:
“And the dead in Christ will rise first” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Paul does not say “those who used to be in Christ”. Even in death, believers are still in Christ. Death can break almost every bond we know, but it cannot break this one.

Still in Christ

The Thessalonian church was grieving. Some of their members had died, and they feared those loved ones would miss out when Christ returned. Paul answers, “For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:14). The dead are not lost. They “have fallen asleep”, a gentle picture of a body at rest, waiting to be woken. And they are still “in Christ”.

The Westminster Shorter Catechism (question 37), followed by Baptist catechisms, puts it beautifully: “The souls of believers are at their death made perfect in holiness, and do immediately pass into glory; and their bodies, being still united to Christ, do rest in their graves till the resurrection.” Even the body in the grave belongs to Christ. He has not forgotten a single one.

With Christ, which is far better

What of the believer’s soul? Paul had no doubt: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain … My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:21, 23). For the believer, death is not a gap in fellowship with Christ but a nearer fellowship. Some Christians have taught that the soul sleeps unconscious until the resurrection, but this commentary holds that believers go immediately and consciously to be with Christ. The study Death, Dying & Heaven discusses this more fully.

“Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on” (Revelation 14:13). To die in the Lord is to die joined to him. Nothing about dying can take a believer out of Christ’s hands.

Raised because he was raised

The resurrection of believers is tied to Christ’s own resurrection. “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). The firstfruits were the first sheaves of the harvest, the guarantee that the rest would follow. Christ is the first; his people are the harvest.

And the same Spirit who joins us to Christ now will raise our bodies then. “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:11). The Spirit who is the bond of union is also the pledge of resurrection.

The bodies that are buried will be raised changed. “What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). “Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49). In Adam we die; in Christ we shall be made alive.

Revealed with him

For now, our union is hidden. “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:3–4). The world does not see it. Often we do not feel it. But one day it will be seen. “We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Then the bride will be presented to the bridegroom, and the long betrothal will give way to the wedding.

That is what Jesus prayed for: “Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory” (John 17:24). The union that began in eternity, was won at the cross and applied by the Spirit will end where Jesus wants it to end: with his people beside him, for ever.

At the graveside

At the funeral of a faithful church member, the pastor read 1 Thessalonians 4. Her grown son, who had drifted from the faith, stood listening. Afterwards he asked the pastor, “Do you really believe she is still in Christ, even now?” The pastor said yes: she is with him, her body rests in his keeping, and he will raise her. And he added that the same Christ was calling her son to come to him. Some months later the son began attending church again. The words “in Christ” had followed him home.

“Therefore encourage one another with these words” (1 Thessalonians 4:18). Death is still an enemy, and we still grieve. But we do not grieve as those who have no hope, because the dead in Christ are not lost. “Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).

For reflection

What comfort does it give you that “the dead in Christ” are still in Christ? How does Christ’s resurrection as the “firstfruits” shape your hope for your own body? What would it mean to live now in the light of Colossians 3:3–4? Whom could you encourage this week with the hope of 1 Thessalonians 4?
